screens.title: Memory Consistency Models
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what a memory consistency model is, why it matters beyond cache coherence, and how different processor families strike a balance between correctness and performance. Memory consistency is the contract that tells you which reorderings of loads and stores are permitted. Without it, two simple threads can observe surprising results because stores may be buffered or loads may be reordered. We will compare three important points on the design spectrum: Sequential Consistency, which is easiest for reasoning but hardest to implement; Total Store Order, used by x86, which allows loads to bypass earlier stores via a store buffer; and weak relaxed models, used by ARM, Power and modern RISC-V variants, which permit many reorderings and rely on fences and atomic primitives to enforce ordering when needed. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete examples, like the two-processor write/read pattern that exposes surprising outcomes, and the double-checked locking pattern that can break on weak hardware unless fenced. By the end you will understand the programmer-visible guarantees each model delivers, when fences are required, and why hardware designers accept complexity in software to gain performance in silicon. Think about how a single missing fence can allow a partially-constructed object to be observed—it shows why this topic is both practical and subtle.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you will build a precise mental model of memory ordering and how hardware implements it. First, you will explain why memory consistency models are necessary even when cache coherence is present; you will practice tracing small examples where reorderings change observable outcomes, and you will be able to name the failure modes that coherence alone cannot prevent. Second, you will distinguish between sequential consistency, Total Store Order, and weak relaxed models. You will learn the formal claim of sequential consistency, what TSO permits with a store buffer and load bypassing, and what "weak" models allow in terms of load and store reorderings. Third, you will learn the specifics of the x86 TSO model and the ARM-style weak ordering: which reorderings are guaranteed, which require fences, and how data-dependency ordering and same-address ordering provide limited guarantees. Finally, you will analyze performance implications: why weaker models enable optimizations like store buffering and reordering for DRAM locality, and where programming complexity rises so that fences or atomic primitives are necessary. These skills prepare you to read ISA manuals and reason about correctness of concurrent algorithms on real processors.

screens.title: How you'll practice these skills
screens.narratorSegment: You will practice by tracing small examples, labeling each memory action with when it becomes visible to other cores, and by writing a compact simulator. Begin by enumerating outcomes for a two-processor example that writes two variables on one core and reads them on another. Use the simulator to show which outcomes each model permits and why. Next, examine the store buffer in TSO: simulate how a store can sit in the buffer, when a local load can read it, and when other processors observe it. Then practice introducing fences and observe how they remove weak outcomes. Finally, apply your understanding to a practical concurrency pattern, such as double-checked locking. Show how a missing fence can expose a partially-constructed object, and how adding the correct fence restores safety. These exercises build both intuition and the ability to decide where hardware guarantees are enough and where explicit synchronization is required. You will finish by explaining trade-offs: which model a given system should choose and what libraries must do to remain portable.

screens.title: Memory Consistency vs Cache Coherence
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define two closely related but distinct ideas: cache coherence and memory consistency. Cache coherence ensures that every memory location has a single, up-to-date value visible across caches — it answers the question, "If two cores read the same address, will they eventually see the same value?" Memory consistency, by contrast, specifies the allowable ordering of memory operations across all processors: it is the contract that determines which interleavings of loads and stores are permissible. Coherence does not prevent reorderings of operations on different addresses, nor does it constrain the moment when a store becomes visible to other processors. That gap creates surprising observable behaviors in multithreaded programs. For example, one core may write A then B, while another core reads B then A. Coherence guarantees they will eventually agree on the values of A and B, but it does not by itself forbid the second core from seeing B=1 and A=0 if reorderings and propagation delays allow it. A common misconception is to assume coherence implies a global program order; it does not. In practice, hardware and ISA memory models close that gap by limiting reorderings or by exposing fences and atomic operations so programmers can restore ordering when needed. The core takeaway is this: you must reason about ordering rules, not just coherence, to guarantee correctness of concurrent code.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Cache coherence keeps values consistent; memory consistency constrains the allowed orderings of accesses and defines the programmer-visible execution behavior.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Memory Consistency vs Coherence
What coherence guarantees
  • Coherence ensures a single, latest value per address is visible across caches eventually.
  • It enforces same-address order: writes to the same address are serialized.
  • It does not say when stores become visible to other cores relative to unrelated loads/stores.
Common misconception
Believing coherence implies a global program order is incorrect; coherence is necessary but not sufficient for predictable multithreaded semantics.
What memory consistency adds
  • Consistency defines allowed reorderings and the global interleaving programmers can rely on.
  • It tells whether a load may see a value before an earlier store becomes visible to other cores.
  • It provides fences or atomic guarantees so programmers can enforce order when needed.
Analogy

Think of coherence as everyone using the same map of addresses; consistency is the traffic law that says which cars may pass each other.

Example
P1: A=1; B=1 — P2: R1=B; R2=A. Coherence alone cannot rule out R1=1,R2=0.
Why it matters
Correct concurrent algorithms must assume the ISA's memory model, not just coherence.
Takeaway
Always consult the memory model when reasoning about multithreaded behavior.

screens.title: Why consistency matters: tracing a two-processor example
screens.narratorSegment: We will trace a compact two-processor example that exposes why memory ordering matters. Processor P1 executes two stores in program order: write A then write B. Processor P2 executes two loads: read B then read A. Ask: what values can P2 observe for its two registers? The process to decide this is: first, list program order constraints for each thread; second, consider allowable hardware reorderings; third, account for when stores propagate to other cores or remain buffered; fourth, enumerate interleavings that respect per-thread ordering and permitted reorderings. Under sequential consistency, the operations of both processors appear in some global sequential order that preserves program order per thread, which forbids the result R1=1, R2=0. Under TSO, store-store order is preserved, loads and loads are ordered, but a load can bypass a prior local store to a different address because stores may sit in a store buffer. That still prevents R1=1, R2=0 here when stores are to different addresses because store-store order ensures S1 comes before S2 globally. Under a weak model, however, stores and loads may be freely reordered across different addresses; writes can be delayed and observed out of order on other cores. This process shows why simply knowing that caches are coherent is not enough: you must enumerate how each model constrains interleavings. A practical check is to run a small simulator and confirm which outcomes each model allows.

keyIdea.title: Tracing process
keyIdea.text: To reason about outcomes, enumerate program order, hardware reorderings, propagation delays, and then list legal interleavings under the model.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Trace: P1 & P2
Trace steps
1. List program order
P1: S1(A), S2(B). P2: L1(B), L2(A).
2. Consider reorderings
Which operations the model allows to pass each other or buffer.
3. Consider propagation
Stores may be buffered and become visible later to other cores.
Enumerated outcomes
  • R1=0, R2=0 — both reads see initial values.
  • R1=1, R2=1 — both stores visible before reads.
  • R1=1, R2=0 — possible on weak models when stores are reordered or visibility delayed.
  • R1=0, R2=1 — possible with different interleavings or buffering.
Example check

Key takeaway
Mechanical enumeration reveals which model permits which surprising behavior.

screens.title: Sequential Consistency (SC)
screens.narratorSegment: Sequential consistency, introduced by Lamport, is the easiest model for programmers to understand because it guarantees that the execution is equivalent to some global sequential ordering of all operations that preserves each processor’s program order. Concretely, that means every load and store appears somewhere in a single interleaving of all threads, and each thread’s own operations appear in program order within that interleaving. The benefit is predictability: if you reason about your program assuming operations happen in program order, SC supports that reasoning directly. The downside is that SC forbids many hardware optimizations: stores cannot be buffered because they must complete immediately and become visible globally; loads cannot bypass previous stores even to different addresses; and aggressive out-of-order execution must be constrained so that memory operations commit in program order. That imposes performance costs and complexity in high-frequency pipelines and memory controllers. Because of those costs, few modern processors implement pure SC at the hardware level. A useful contrast to check is that while SC prevents the surprising outcome R1=1, R2=0 in our example, TSO and weak models relax rules to allow better performance but demand more care from programmers. Keep in mind: SC is a simple mental model, but it is often sacrificed in hardware to gain speed and efficiency.

keyIdea.title: Sequential Consistency
keyIdea.text: SC preserves program order and presents a single global interleaving of all operations, trading hardware flexibility for programmer simplicity.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Sequential Consistency
Sequential Consistency
A single global order that preserves per-thread program order.
Formal rules
  • Result equals some sequential interleaving of all processors' operations.
  • Each processor's operations appear in program order in that interleaving.
Because of this, programmers can reason linearly about memory effects without inserting fences.
Hardware cost
  • Prevents store buffering and many out-of-order optimizations.
  • Requires strong ordering of memory commits, reducing throughput and latency hiding.
Most high-performance ISAs choose weaker models to avoid these costs.
Analogy
All cars follow a single lane — no passing allowed.
Example
Under SC, R1=1,R2=0 from our example cannot occur; program order must be preserved in the global view.
Takeaway
SC is simple for reasoning but expensive for fast hardware.

screens.title: Total Store Order (TSO) and the Store Buffer
screens.narratorSegment: Total Store Order, the memory model used by x86 processors, relaxes sequential consistency in a carefully constrained way that enables high performance while keeping programming relatively simple. The central mechanism is the store buffer: when a processor issues a store, the value is placed into the local store buffer and the C P U proceeds without waiting for the store to become visible in the cache hierarchy. Loads from the same processor can read from that store buffer or bypass earlier buffered stores to different addresses. This permits load-store reordering: a later load to a different address may complete before an earlier store is globally visible. TSO preserves store-store and load-load ordering, so stores remain ordered with respect to each other and loads maintain their program order. That combination prevents many of the counterintuitive outcomes that are possible on weak models. A concrete consequence is that many common multithreaded programs written for x86 behave correctly without explicit fences. The typical misconception is that buffering always breaks correctness; in practice TSO provides strong enough guarantees for most synchronization idioms while benefiting from store buffering to improve throughput. When stricter ordering is needed, x86 exposes fence instructions such as MFENCE that flush the store buffer and restore stronger ordering.

keyIdea.title: TSO summary
keyIdea.text: TSO uses a store buffer to allow loads to bypass earlier stores to other addresses, preserving store-store and load-load order but relaxing load-store ordering.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › TSO & Store Buffer
TSO: practical compromise
Store buffer enables write buffering; loads may bypass earlier stores to other addresses.
Store buffer behavior
  • Stores are placed in a local buffer and later propagated to cache/memory.
  • Local loads may read from the buffer, enabling the issuing core to see its own writes early.
This allows the CPU to continue without stalling for global visibility.
Ordering guarantees
  • Store-store order preserved.
  • Load-load order preserved.
  • Load may bypass earlier store to a different address (load-store reordering).
Fence instructions flush buffers to enforce ordering when required.
Illustration
Imagine a loading dock where outgoing trucks wait before entering the main road; local drivers can read from trucks in the dock immediately.
Example
x86 programs usually work without explicit fences because TSO preserves many useful orderings.
Takeaway
TSO balances hardware optimizations and programmer convenience using a store buffer.

screens.title: Can TSO produce R1=1, R2=0?
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a focused question: given P1 performs A=1 then B=1 and P2 performs R1=B then R2=A, can x86 TSO produce the outcome R1 equals 1 and R2 equals 0? To answer, consider TSO guarantees: stores preserve their mutual order, loads preserve order with each other, and loads may bypass earlier stores to different addresses thanks to the store buffer. In our example, the two stores on P1 are ordered S1 then S2; because store-store order is preserved, any global interleaving must keep S1 before S2. For P2 to observe R1=1, it must see the effect of S2 before its own L2. But if P2 sees B=1, that implies S2 has become visible to P2; since S1 precedes S2 on P1 and store-store order is preserved, S1 must also have been issued before S2 and cannot appear after S2 in global order. The remaining subtlety is store propagation delays: could S2 be propagated to P2 before S1? Under TSO, stores maintain order in visibility — store-store ordering is preserved globally, meaning other processors cannot see S2 while missing S1. Therefore R1=1 and R2=0 is not possible on TSO. A common mistake is to conflate "store buffering" with arbitrary reordering across other cores; buffering allows local progress but does not violate the preserved store-store order that prevents this particular outcome. This reasoning shows how TSO keeps many intuitive properties while still allowing valuable optimizations.

keyIdea.title: TSO outcome
keyIdea.text: Under TSO, R1=1,R2=0 from the two-store/two-load example is impossible because store-store order preserves visibility of S1 before S2 to other processors.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › TSO Outcome Reasoning
Step-by-step comparison
Key constraints
  • Store-store ordering preserved globally.
  • Load may bypass earlier local stores to other addresses.
Implication
If S2 is visible, S1 must also be visible because S1 precedes S2 on P1.
Consequence

R1=1,R2=0 cannot occur on TSO; store-store ordering prevents that weak outcome.

Misconception
Store buffering means everything can reorder — not true for store-store ordering under TSO.
Check
Enumerate the global order preserving per-thread orders; you will see S1 cannot be after S2.
Takeaway
TSO gives strong intuitive guarantees while enabling buffering optimizations.

screens.title: Weak / Relaxed Memory Models
screens.narratorSegment: Weak or relaxed memory models, used by ARM, PowerPC, and some RISC-V variants, allow many more reorderings of loads and stores to different addresses than TSO or SC. In these models, loads may be reordered with other loads, stores may be reordered with other stores, and stores and loads can cross in either direction unless the model provides explicit constraints. The common guarantees retained are limited: same-address ordering is usually preserved so accesses to the same address appear consistent, and data-dependency ordering is often preserved so a load whose address depends on a prior load will respect that dependence. These limited guarantees let the hardware perform aggressive optimizations: issue loads early to hide latency, buffer and merge stores for bandwidth efficiency, and reorder transactions to improve DRAM throughput. The trade-off is programming difficulty: concurrent code must use explicit synchronization primitives or fences to ensure ordering. A classic consequence is that lock-free patterns that are safe on TSO or under SC can be broken on weak models unless they employ proper fences. A good mental model is to think of the hardware as allowing cars to pass at intersections unless a traffic cop (a fence) intervenes. The key skill is recognizing where fences are required to restore the higher-level ordering your algorithm depends on.

keyIdea.title: Weak models
keyIdea.text: Weak models maximize hardware performance by allowing many reorderings; they keep limited guarantees like data-dependency and same-address ordering and rely on fences for stronger behavior.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Weak / Relaxed Models
Relaxed ordering for performance
ARM, Power and many RISC-V variants expose weak guarantees to enable hardware optimizations.
Allowed reorderings
  • Load-load reordering may occur.
  • Store-store reordering may occur.
  • Load-store and store-load reorderings are commonly allowed.
Only same-address and data-dependency orderings are commonly preserved without fences.
Programming consequences
  • Fences are required to prevent reordering in synchronization code.
  • Compilers and libraries must map higher-level synchronization to correct fences and atomics.
Lock-free algorithms often need careful fence placement on weak models.
Analogy
Intersections with no lights: drivers can pass unless a cop (fence) stops them.
Example caution
Double-checked locking requires fences to avoid publication before construction finishes.
Takeaway
Weak models give speed but make correctness rely on explicit synchronization.

screens.title: Double-checked locking and fences
screens.narratorSegment: Double-checked locking is a classic pattern where a pointer is tested without a lock, then the lock is taken and tested again before initializing a singleton. On weak memory models, a missing fence in this pattern can allow the pointer store to become visible to other cores before the constructor has completed, so another thread may observe a pointer to a partially initialized object. The safe approach on weak hardware is to insert a store-store fence or an equivalent atomic operation that enforces the required ordering so that the store that publishes the pointer cannot be observed until prior writes to the object's fields are globally visible. Look at the provided snippet: the allocation and construction must complete before ptr is assigned. screens.title: Memory Fences and Barriers
screens.narratorSegment: Memory fences are explicit instructions that prevent certain classes of reorderings across the fence. There are several common types: load-load fences prevent later loads from passing earlier loads; store-store fences prevent later stores from passing earlier stores; load-store or store-load fences block cross-type reorderings in one direction; and a full fence prevents all reorderings across it. The precise names and effects vary by ISA, but the conceptual role is the same: a fence enforces that memory operations prior to the fence become visible in the order required before operations after the fence are allowed to proceed in a way that could be observed by other processors. High-level synchronization primitives like mutexes and atomic operations typically include the necessary fence semantics so programmers don't manage raw fences directly. When to use fences? Use them in low-level lock-free algorithms, in publish-subscribe patterns where one core publishes initialized state to others, and to implement ordering requirements that the compiler or hardware might otherwise violate. A common pitfall is inserting the wrong kind of fence: a weaker fence might not prevent the reordering you care about. Always consult the ISA documentation or use well-tested atomic primitives that express the intended acquire/release semantics rather than hand-choosing fence types. The goal is to enforce the minimum necessary ordering to avoid performance loss while maintaining correctness.

screens.title: Performance vs Programmability
screens.narratorSegment: Different memory models trade programmer convenience for hardware performance. Sequential consistency offers the simplest mental model — programmers can assume a single global interleaving that preserves program order — but it forces hardware to forbid buffering and reordering that hide latency or increase throughput, resulting in lower performance. Total Store Order, used by x86, relaxes SC by allowing loads to bypass earlier stores, gaining substantial performance via store buffers while still preserving key ordering properties that make most programs straightforward to reason about. Weak models maximize flexibility: they allow nearly all reorderings across different addresses, enabling more aggressive instruction reordering, store merging, and reordering of memory traffic to improve DRAM utilization and power efficiency. The cost of weak models is higher programming difficulty: developers must reason about fences and rely on atomics and library primitives. From a practical standpoint, architects choose a model that fits their targets: high-performance server processors often accept stronger models for easier programming, while mobile and embedded processors emphasize power and throughput and therefore use weaker models. A useful practical rule is: use the ISA's provided atomic and synchronization primitives rather than assuming intuitive ordering, and measure performance to justify stronger fences only when necessary. Understanding the trade-off helps you make correct design choices in both hardware-aware software and low-level system libraries.

Sequential Consistency

screens.title: Simulator: enumerate outcomes for SC, TSO, and Weak
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity is to write a small Python simulator that enumerates possible outcomes of a simple multithreaded program under three memory models: SC, TSO, and a weak model. The simulator should represent each processor as a sequence of ordered operations and model the store buffer and propagation rules for TSO. For SC, generate all global interleavings that preserve each thread's program order and evaluate the reads. For TSO, model each core's store buffer: stores go to the buffer and become visible to others only when drained; local loads may read from the buffer or memory and can bypass buffered stores to other addresses. For the weak model, allow reorderings of loads and stores to different addresses, but preserve same-address and data-dependency ordering. Run the example with P1 doing A=1;B=1 and P2 doing R1=B;R2=A. Show that SC and TSO never produce R1=1,R2=0, but the weak model can. Then add a memory fence after S1 and show that it removes the weak outcome by preventing the store from being observed out of order. This exercise enforces the mechanical thinking necessary to understand models and produces evidence you can inspect. As you implement, check corner cases: reading from the store buffer locally, and ensuring same-address ordering in the weak model.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three compact, high-value facts you should remember. First: memory consistency and cache coherence are different; coherence guarantees a single latest value per address, while consistency specifies the ordering rules processors and compilers must follow or expose. Second: sequential consistency gives a single global interleaving that preserves program order and is easiest to reason about, but it prevents important hardware optimizations. Third: TSO and weak models represent practical compromises — TSO uses a store buffer to allow load bypassing while preserving store-store order, and weak models allow broad reordering but preserve same-address and data-dependency ordering, requiring fences or atomic operations for safety. Keep these three points in mind when you read ISA documentation or reason about concurrency: know which model your target uses, prefer high-level synchronization primitives that express ordering correctly, and use simulation or formal reasoning to validate tricky lock-free code. A final reflective question: when you design a concurrent algorithm, which assumptions about ordering are safe to make and which require explicit fencing?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what a memory consistency model is, why it matters beyond cache coherence, and how different processor families strike a balance between correctness and performance. Memory consistency is the contract that tells you which reorderings of loads and stores are permitted. Without it, two simple threads can observe surprising results because stores may be buffered or loads may be reordered. We will compare three important points on the design spectrum: Sequential Consistency, which is easiest for reasoning but hardest to implement; Total Store Order, used by x86, which allows loads to bypass earlier stores via a store buffer; and weak relaxed models, used by ARM, Power and modern RISC-V variants, which permit many reorderings and rely on fences and atomic primitives to enforce ordering when needed. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete examples, like the two-processor write/read pattern that exposes surprising outcomes, and the double-checked locking pattern that can break on weak hardware unless fenced. By the end you will understand the programmer-visible guarantees each model delivers, when fences are required, and why hardware designers accept complexity in software to gain performance in silicon. Think about how a single missing fence can allow a partially-constructed object to be observed—it shows why this topic is both practical and subtle.

In this module you will build a precise mental model of memory ordering and how hardware implements it. First, you will explain why memory consistency models are necessary even when cache coherence is present; you will practice tracing small examples where reorderings change observable outcomes, and you will be able to name the failure modes that coherence alone cannot prevent. Second, you will distinguish between sequential consistency, Total Store Order, and weak relaxed models. You will learn the formal claim of sequential consistency, what TSO permits with a store buffer and load bypassing, and what "weak" models allow in terms of load and store reorderings. Third, you will learn the specifics of the x86 TSO model and the ARM-style weak ordering: which reorderings are guaranteed, which require fences, and how data-dependency ordering and same-address ordering provide limited guarantees. Finally, you will analyze performance implications: why weaker models enable optimizations like store buffering and reordering for DRAM locality, and where programming complexity rises so that fences or atomic primitives are necessary. These skills prepare you to read ISA manuals and reason about correctness of concurrent algorithms on real processors.

You will practice by tracing small examples, labeling each memory action with when it becomes visible to other cores, and by writing a compact simulator. Begin by enumerating outcomes for a two-processor example that writes two variables on one core and reads them on another. Use the simulator to show which outcomes each model permits and why. Next, examine the store buffer in TSO: simulate how a store can sit in the buffer, when a local load can read it, and when other processors observe it. Then practice introducing fences and observe how they remove weak outcomes. Finally, apply your understanding to a practical concurrency pattern, such as double-checked locking. Show how a missing fence can expose a partially-constructed object, and how adding the correct fence restores safety. These exercises build both intuition and the ability to decide where hardware guarantees are enough and where explicit synchronization is required. You will finish by explaining trade-offs: which model a given system should choose and what libraries must do to remain portable.

Let's define two closely related but distinct ideas: cache coherence and memory consistency. Cache coherence ensures that every memory location has a single, up-to-date value visible across caches — it answers the question, "If two cores read the same address, will they eventually see the same value?" Memory consistency, by contrast, specifies the allowable ordering of memory operations across all processors: it is the contract that determines which interleavings of loads and stores are permissible. Coherence does not prevent reorderings of operations on different addresses, nor does it constrain the moment when a store becomes visible to other processors. That gap creates surprising observable behaviors in multithreaded programs. For example, one core may write A then B, while another core reads B then A. Coherence guarantees they will eventually agree on the values of A and B, but it does not by itself forbid the second core from seeing B=1 and A=0 if reorderings and propagation delays allow it. A common misconception is to assume coherence implies a global program order; it does not. In practice, hardware and ISA memory models close that gap by limiting reorderings or by exposing fences and atomic operations so programmers can restore ordering when needed. The core takeaway is this: you must reason about ordering rules, not just coherence, to guarantee correctness of concurrent code.

We will trace a compact two-processor example that exposes why memory ordering matters. Processor P1 executes two stores in program order: write A then write B. Processor P2 executes two loads: read B then read A. Ask: what values can P2 observe for its two registers? The process to decide this is: first, list program order constraints for each thread; second, consider allowable hardware reorderings; third, account for when stores propagate to other cores or remain buffered; fourth, enumerate interleavings that respect per-thread ordering and permitted reorderings. Under sequential consistency, the operations of both processors appear in some global sequential order that preserves program order per thread, which forbids the result R1=1, R2=0. Under TSO, store-store order is preserved, loads and loads are ordered, but a load can bypass a prior local store to a different address because stores may sit in a store buffer. That still prevents R1=1, R2=0 here when stores are to different addresses because store-store order ensures S1 comes before S2 globally. Under a weak model, however, stores and loads may be freely reordered across different addresses; writes can be delayed and observed out of order on other cores. This process shows why simply knowing that caches are coherent is not enough: you must enumerate how each model constrains interleavings. A practical check is to run a small simulator and confirm which outcomes each model allows.

Sequential consistency, introduced by Lamport, is the easiest model for programmers to understand because it guarantees that the execution is equivalent to some global sequential ordering of all operations that preserves each processor’s program order. Concretely, that means every load and store appears somewhere in a single interleaving of all threads, and each thread’s own operations appear in program order within that interleaving. The benefit is predictability: if you reason about your program assuming operations happen in program order, SC supports that reasoning directly. The downside is that SC forbids many hardware optimizations: stores cannot be buffered because they must complete immediately and become visible globally; loads cannot bypass previous stores even to different addresses; and aggressive out-of-order execution must be constrained so that memory operations commit in program order. That imposes performance costs and complexity in high-frequency pipelines and memory controllers. Because of those costs, few modern processors implement pure SC at the hardware level. A useful contrast to check is that while SC prevents the surprising outcome R1=1, R2=0 in our example, TSO and weak models relax rules to allow better performance but demand more care from programmers. Keep in mind: SC is a simple mental model, but it is often sacrificed in hardware to gain speed and efficiency.

Total Store Order, the memory model used by x86 processors, relaxes sequential consistency in a carefully constrained way that enables high performance while keeping programming relatively simple. The central mechanism is the store buffer: when a processor issues a store, the value is placed into the local store buffer and the C P U proceeds without waiting for the store to become visible in the cache hierarchy. Loads from the same processor can read from that store buffer or bypass earlier buffered stores to different addresses. This permits load-store reordering: a later load to a different address may complete before an earlier store is globally visible. TSO preserves store-store and load-load ordering, so stores remain ordered with respect to each other and loads maintain their program order. That combination prevents many of the counterintuitive outcomes that are possible on weak models. A concrete consequence is that many common multithreaded programs written for x86 behave correctly without explicit fences. The typical misconception is that buffering always breaks correctness; in practice TSO provides strong enough guarantees for most synchronization idioms while benefiting from store buffering to improve throughput. When stricter ordering is needed, x86 exposes fence instructions such as MFENCE that flush the store buffer and restore stronger ordering.

Here is a focused question: given P1 performs A=1 then B=1 and P2 performs R1=B then R2=A, can x86 TSO produce the outcome R1 equals 1 and R2 equals 0? To answer, consider TSO guarantees: stores preserve their mutual order, loads preserve order with each other, and loads may bypass earlier stores to different addresses thanks to the store buffer. In our example, the two stores on P1 are ordered S1 then S2; because store-store order is preserved, any global interleaving must keep S1 before S2. For P2 to observe R1=1, it must see the effect of S2 before its own L2. But if P2 sees B=1, that implies S2 has become visible to P2; since S1 precedes S2 on P1 and store-store order is preserved, S1 must also have been issued before S2 and cannot appear after S2 in global order. The remaining subtlety is store propagation delays: could S2 be propagated to P2 before S1? Under TSO, stores maintain order in visibility — store-store ordering is preserved globally, meaning other processors cannot see S2 while missing S1. Therefore R1=1 and R2=0 is not possible on TSO. A common mistake is to conflate "store buffering" with arbitrary reordering across other cores; buffering allows local progress but does not violate the preserved store-store order that prevents this particular outcome. This reasoning shows how TSO keeps many intuitive properties while still allowing valuable optimizations.

Weak or relaxed memory models, used by ARM, PowerPC, and some RISC-V variants, allow many more reorderings of loads and stores to different addresses than TSO or SC. In these models, loads may be reordered with other loads, stores may be reordered with other stores, and stores and loads can cross in either direction unless the model provides explicit constraints. The common guarantees retained are limited: same-address ordering is usually preserved so accesses to the same address appear consistent, and data-dependency ordering is often preserved so a load whose address depends on a prior load will respect that dependence. These limited guarantees let the hardware perform aggressive optimizations: issue loads early to hide latency, buffer and merge stores for bandwidth efficiency, and reorder transactions to improve DRAM throughput. A classic consequence is that lock-free patterns that are safe on TSO or under SC can be broken on weak models unless they employ proper fences. A good mental model is to think of the hardware as allowing cars to pass at intersections unless a traffic cop (a fence) intervenes. The key skill is recognizing where fences are required to restore the higher-level ordering your algorithm depends on.

Always consult the ISA documentation or use well-tested atomic primitives that express the intended acquire/release semantics rather than hand-choosing fence types. Let's summarize three compact, high-value facts you should remember. First: memory consistency and cache coherence are different; coherence guarantees a single latest value per address, while consistency specifies the ordering rules processors and compilers must follow or expose. Second: sequential consistency gives a single global interleaving that preserves program order and is easiest to reason about, but it prevents important hardware optimizations. Third: TSO and weak models represent practical compromises — TSO uses a store buffer to allow load bypassing while preserving store-store order, and weak models allow broad reordering but preserve same-address and data-dependency ordering, requiring fences or atomic operations for safety. Keep these three points in mind when you read ISA documentation or reason about concurrency: know which model your target uses, prefer high-level synchronization primitives that express ordering correctly, and use simulation or formal reasoning to validate tricky lock-free code. One last quick reference you can carry into coding or reading architecture manuals. First: store buffers let a core make progress by delaying global visibility of stores; always consider whether other cores can observe a store before its predecessors. Second: data-dependency and same-address ordering provide limited natural ordering in weak models; do not rely on full program order unless the model guarantees it. Third: fences and atomic primitives are the right tools to enforce ordering; prefer language-provided acquire/release or full-fence operations rather than ad-hoc store instructions. When you design concurrent algorithms or port libraries between ISAs, these concise rules will guide your decisions: simulate tricky interleavings, prefer safe atomics, and minimize fences to the smallest necessary set for correctness.
